source.title: Rethinking the Lisfranc injury: Rationale for and development of a new classification system for Lisfranc injuries

paper.citation: Cawley W.C., Hwang P., Mittal R., Zochowski Y., Darwish I., O’Keefe R., et al. Rethinking the Lisfranc injury: Rationale for and development of a new classification system for Lisfranc injuries. Injury. 2026;57(8):113422. doi:10.1016/j.injury.2026.113422.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Does the newly developed Suthersan classification produce better inter- and intra-rater agreement than the Myerson–Hardcastle classification for indirect Lisfranc injuries? The cohort comprised 176 patients older than 16 years with indirect Lisfranc injuries and accessible three-dimensional imaging, treated by one surgeon at an Australian tertiary trauma hospital from 2018 to 2024. Mean age was 41.6 years and 45.5% were female. This was a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected surgical-database data. The proposed system classifies indirect injuries by the entry and propagation of force, distinguishing lesser-arc from greater-arc patterns.
paper.tldr: Combined inter-rater kappa was 0.95 for the Suthersan classification and 0.65 for Myerson–Hardcastle. Suthersan intra-rater agreement was 96.6%, 96.6%, and 100% across the three raters, compared with 74.1%, 96.6%, and 92.9% for Myerson–Hardcastle. The classification can structure specialist discussion of indirect Lisfranc morphology and prompt review of the wider midfoot on CT.
paper.methods: This was a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected surgical-database data. The proposed system classifies indirect injuries by the entry and propagation of force, distinguishing lesser-arc from greater-arc patterns. Two fellowship-trained foot-and-ankle surgeons and one hand surgeon independently classified blinded imaging with both systems. A subset was reclassified after six months; Cohen's kappa summarized agreement.
paper.findings: Combined inter-rater kappa was 0.95 for the Suthersan classification and 0.65 for Myerson–Hardcastle. Suthersan intra-rater agreement was 96.6%, 96.6%, and 100% across the three raters, compared with 74.1%, 96.6%, and 92.9% for Myerson–Hardcastle. Nineteen of 176 CT scans, or 10.8%, were not classifiable with the Myerson system. About 14% of injuries involved the navicular, talus, naviculocuneiform joint, or talonavicular joint, supporting broader midfoot assessment in this series. In the small outcome subset, median AOFAS score did not significantly differ between grade 1 and grades 2–4.
paper.limitations: The system was developed by one surgeon and tested on that surgeon's single-center case series, creating incorporation and preference risks. Approximately 20% of identified indirect injuries lacked accessible imaging, only three surgeons rated scans, and race, ethnicity, and sex/gender subgroup analyses were unavailable. Crush injuries were excluded, image quality may have affected classification, and clinical outcome correlation was outside the main study scope. High agreement does not establish diagnostic accuracy, prognostic value, treatment effectiveness, or return-to-sport guidance.
paper.practicalImplications: The classification can structure specialist discussion of indirect Lisfranc morphology and prompt review of the wider midfoot on CT. It should not yet drive fixation strategy, prognosis, or return-to-play by grade alone. In athlete care, use it alongside mechanism, weight-bearing imaging when appropriate, symptoms, instability, specialist examination, and functional progression. Prospective, multi-center studies with broader raters and patient outcomes are needed before treating its categories as management algorithms.
